title: Thread pool — why, how, Executors types (fixed, cached, single, scheduled)
shortTitle: Thread pool — why, how, Executors types (fixed, cached, single, scheduled)

s1_definition.profdef: A **thread pool** is a collection of pre-created, reusable worker threads managed by an `ExecutorService`. Instead of creating a new thread for each task (`new Thread().start()`), you SUBMIT tasks to the pool — an idle worker picks it up, executes it, then becomes available for the next task. Benefits: (1) **Reuse** — thread creation cost (~1ms, ~1MB stack) paid once, not per-task. (2) **Bounded concurrency** — fixed pool size prevents OOM from unlimited threads. (3) **Task queueing** — excess tasks wait in a queue until a worker is free. (4) **Lifecycle management** — `shutdown()` gracefully stops the pool. Types: `newFixedThreadPool(n)` — n workers, unbounded queue. `newCachedThreadPool()` — 0 to Integer.MAX threads, 60s idle timeout. `newSingleThreadExecutor()` — 1 worker, tasks execute sequentially. `newScheduledThreadPool(n)` — n workers for delayed/periodic tasks.
s1_definition.analogy: Creating a new thread per task = hiring a NEW teller for every customer, then FIRING them after one transaction. 10,000 customers = 10,000 hires + fires. Absurd! Thread pool = hiring 10 PERMANENT tellers at branch opening. Customers queue up. Each teller serves one customer, then takes the next from the queue. 10 tellers serve 10,000 customers throughout the day. **Fixed pool** = exactly 10 tellers, always. **Cached pool** = tellers hired on demand, fired after 60 seconds of idleness. **Single** = one teller (sequential). **Scheduled** = tellers who can schedule appointments (delayed/periodic).
s1_definition.oneliner: Thread pool = pre-created reusable threads + task queue. Fixed (predictable), Cached (elastic), Single (sequential), Scheduled (delayed/periodic). NEVER new Thread() in production — always use a pool.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A **thread pool** is a collection of pre-created, reusable worker threads managed by an `ExecutorService`. Instead of creating a new thread for each task (`new Thread().start()`), you SUBMIT tasks to the pool — an idle worker picks it up, executes it, then becomes available for the next task. Benefits: (1) **Reuse** — thread creation cost (~1ms, ~1MB stack) paid once, not per-task. (2) **Bounded concurrency** — fixed pool size prevents OOM from unlimited threads. (3) **Task queueing** — excess tasks wait in a queue until a worker is free. (4) **Lifecycle management** — `shutdown()` gracefully stops the pool. Types: `newFixedThreadPool(n)` — n workers, unbounded queue. `newCachedThreadPool()` — 0 to Integer.MAX threads, 60s idle timeout. `newSingleThreadExecutor()` — 1 worker, tasks execute sequentially. `newScheduledThreadPool(n)` — n workers for delayed/periodic tasks.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Creating a new thread per task = hiring a NEW teller for every customer, then FIRING them after one transaction. 10,000 customers = 10,000 hires + fires. Absurd! Thread pool = hiring 10 PERMANENT tellers at branch opening. Customers queue up. Each teller serves one customer, then takes the next from the queue. 10 tellers serve 10,000 customers throughout the day. **Fixed pool** = exactly 10 tellers, always. **Cached pool** = tellers hired on demand, fired after 60 seconds of idleness. **Single** = one teller (sequential). **Scheduled** = tellers who can schedule appointments (delayed/periodic).

**One line to remember:** Thread pool = pre-created reusable threads + task queue. Fixed (predictable), Cached (elastic), Single (sequential), Scheduled (delayed/periodic). NEVER new Thread() in production — always use a pool.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade notification service created `new Thread()` for every notification.** 50K trades/day × 3 notifications each (SMS, email, push) = 150K threads created and destroyed daily. Memory spikes, GC pressure, OOM during peak. Fix: `newFixedThreadPool(20)` for notifications. 20 threads handle 150K tasks via queue. Thread creation: 20 (once) instead of 150K. Memory: 20MB instead of 150GB. Added: custom ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue (1000) + CallerRunsPolicy (back-pressure when queue full).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `newFixedThreadPool(3)` creates 3 worker threads. They start IDLE, waiting for tasks from the internal `LinkedBlockingQueue`.

**Step 2.** 30 tasks submitted via `pool.submit()`. First 3 go to workers immediately. Remaining 27 queued.

**Step 3.** Worker-1 finishes task-1 → takes task-4 from queue. Worker-2 finishes task-2 → takes task-5. Continuous cycle until all 30 done.

**Step 4.** Only 3 threads created total. Each thread executed ~10 tasks. Thread creation cost: 3 × ~1ms = 3ms. Without pool: 30 × ~1ms = 30ms + 30MB stack vs 3MB.

**Step 5.** `pool.shutdown()` → stops accepting new tasks → workers finish remaining queued tasks → all threads terminate.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ THREAD POOL ARCHITECTURE ═══

  submit(task) → [Task Queue (LinkedBlockingQueue)]
                         ↓         ↓         ↓
                  [Worker-1] [Worker-2] [Worker-3]
                  execute     execute    execute
                  done→take   done→take  done→take
                  next task   next task  next task

  ═══ POOL TYPES ═══
  Fixed(10):      10 workers, unbounded queue, predictable
  Cached:         0→∞ workers, 60s idle timeout, elastic
  Single:         1 worker, sequential, ordered
  Scheduled:      N workers, delayed/periodic tasks
  Custom(TPE):    core/max/queue/reject → full control!

  ═══ DANGER: Executors factory methods ═══
  newFixedThreadPool:  unbounded queue → OOM if tasks pile up!
  newCachedThreadPool: unbounded threads → OOM under load!
  FIX: use ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue + rejection policy
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ThreadPoolExecutor Internals ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ThreadPoolExecutor                       │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - corePoolSize: int     (min workers)   │
  │  - maxPoolSize: int      (max workers)   │
  │  - keepAliveTime: long   (idle timeout)  │
  │  - workQueue: BlockingQueue<Runnable>    │
  │  - threadFactory: ThreadFactory          │
  │  - rejectionHandler: RejectedHandler     │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + submit(Callable): Future              │
  │  + execute(Runnable): void               │
  │  + shutdown(): void                      │
  │  + shutdownNow(): List<Runnable>         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Task submission flow:
  1. workers < corePoolSize → create new worker thread
  2. workers >= core → add to workQueue
  3. queue full + workers < maxPoolSize → create new thread
  4. queue full + workers >= max → REJECT (RejectedExecutionHandler)

  Rejection policies:
  AbortPolicy:      throw RejectedExecutionException (default)
  CallerRunsPolicy: caller thread executes the task (back-pressure!)
  DiscardPolicy:    silently discard the task
  DiscardOldest:    discard oldest queued task, retry submit
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A thread pool pre-creates reusable worker threads managed by ExecutorService. Benefits: thread reuse (creation cost paid once), bounded concurrency (no OOM from unlimited threads), task queueing (excess work waits), and lifecycle management (graceful shutdown). Four types: `newFixedThreadPool(n)` for predictable workloads, `newCachedThreadPool()` for elastic short-lived tasks, `newSingleThreadExecutor()` for sequential processing, and `newScheduledThreadPool(n)` for delayed/periodic tasks.

In production: NEVER use Executors factory methods directly — they create unbounded queues or unbounded thread counts → OOM risk. Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` directly with bounded queue and rejection policy. Core/max pool size tuning: CPU-bound tasks → core count threads. IO-bound tasks → core count × 2-4 threads. Always specify: `new ThreadPoolExecutor(core, max, keepAlive, unit, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(boundedSize), rejectionPolicy)`. In banking: notification service — 20-thread pool handles 150K daily notifications. CallerRunsPolicy as rejection handler: when queue is full, the submitting thread executes the task itself (natural back-pressure).
